waypoints.label: Let people share short blog posts
waypoints.notes: Flaskr is the small blog app built step by step in Flask's tutorial (docs/tutorial/). Users register and log in, then write, edit and delete their own posts; anyone can read them.

waypoints.label: Only the author can change their posts
waypoints.notes: Enforced in two places: login_required (you must be logged in) and get_post's author check in blog.py (you must be the post's author). Tested by test_author_required in tests/test_blog.py.

waypoints.label: Build the app in a factory function
waypoints.notes: create_app(test_config=None) in flaskr/__init__.py builds and returns the app. Tests pass their own config, such as a temporary database (see tests/conftest.py). Rationale: docs/tutorial/factory.rst.

waypoints.label: Split features into blueprints
waypoints.notes: Two blueprints: auth (under /auth) and blog (no prefix, so it serves /). Both are registered in create_app. Rationale: docs/tutorial/views.rst.

waypoints.label: Plain SQLite, no ORM
waypoints.notes: Python's built-in sqlite3 with hand-written SQL. Tables (user, post) are in flaskr/schema.sql; flask init-db creates them. One connection per request, kept on g and closed at teardown. Rationale: docs/tutorial/database.rst.

waypoints.label: Login and registration
waypoints.notes: Passwords are stored hashed (generate_password_hash, line 68). Logging in stores the user's id in the session (line 104); load_logged_in_user (line 32) puts that user in g.user before every request.

waypoints.label: Blog views
waypoints.notes: Routes: / (index), /create, /<id>/update and /<id>/delete. get_post (line 28) returns 404 if the post doesn't exist and 403 if you aren't its author (line 55).

waypoints.label: login_required
waypoints.notes: A decorator in auth.py (line 19): if g.user is None, it redirects to the login page. Used on create, update and delete in blog.py.

waypoints.label: Tests use a fresh app per test
waypoints.notes: The app fixture in conftest.py makes a temporary database file, calls create_app({'TESTING': True, 'DATABASE': db_path}) for each test, then deletes the file. Run pytest from examples/tutorial.

waypoints.label: Default secret key is 'dev'
waypoints.notes: create_app sets SECRET_KEY to 'dev'. The key signs the session cookie, so anyone who knows it could forge a login. docs/tutorial/deploy.rst says to override it in instance/config.py.

tours.author: Claude

stops.narrative: To serve that goal, flaskr makes a few structural decisions. First: how the app gets created.
Because the app is made by a function, tests can make their own. Next: what that buys the tests.
That is the payoff of the factory. Next decision: how the code is divided up.
Each blueprint owns its own routes. Next decision: where the data lives.
Simple choices keep the tutorial small, but some defaults are not safe to ship. Last stop: a risk.
End of the tour. Which of these decisions would you change for a real product, and why?

tours.author: Claude

stops.narrative: A tour is a guided path through a project's map, written by someone who understands it. This first stop is flaskr's goal. Press Next to go on, or Escape to leave the tour at any time. Next: the user need behind the goal.
Goals and user needs are the why: the intent behind the code, which the code itself doesn't record. Next: the feature that meets this need.
Features are what the app does for people. The lines between waypoints are labelled with how they relate, like implemented-by. Next: a design decision behind the code.
An ADR records a decision and why it was made. This one comes from Flask's own docs. Next: the code it led to.
Code waypoints link to their file. Click the file link in the panel to open blog.py on GitHub, or Copy path to find it in your editor. Next: something that could go wrong.
Risks belong on the map too: what someone changing this code should know before they ship it. Next: how the code is tested.
